story: When Apollo 11 returned from the Moon in July 1969, humanity's greatest triumph was met with extreme biological paranoia. Terrified that the crew might introduce lethal lunar pathogens to Earth, NASA placed Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins into a strict 21-day quarantine. Right after splashing down in the Pacific Ocean, the astronauts donned sealed biological isolation garments and entered a converted Airstream trailer known as the Mobile Quarantine Facility aboard the USS Hornet. There, President Nixon greeted them through a sealed glass window. Flown to Houston, they spent the remainder of their isolation inside the Lunar Receiving Laboratory alongside 49 pounds of moon rocks, their spacecraft, and medical personnel. They conducted debriefs behind glass walls and even threw Armstrong a 39th birthday party. After daily health checks confirmed no alien life existed, they were released on August 10, and NASA scrapped the protocol after Apollo 14.
angle: NASA spent millions building airtight quarantine facilities to stop hypothetical Moon plagues, yet the entire barrier was breached the moment divers cracked the hatch in the open ocean.
disputed: BBC Sky at Night states the Apollo 11 crew was isolated for two weeks upon return, whereas NASA, Space.com, ABC News, and Space Center Houston specify the quarantine lasted 21 days from exposure; scripts should use the official 21-day timeline.

The exact number of support staff quarantined alongside the crew varies by source (two in the trailer per S1, about 20 per S3, over a dozen per S4, and 24 per S6); scripts should describe the support staff generally rather than citing a single exact figure.
